items.content_html:
Context

The repository has a small golden-trace regression set, but it is not yet a quality dataset. tests/eval/golden_traces.py currently lists five Langfuse trace IDs—one for several AWS resource-type subgraphs—and tests/eval/test_eval_regression.py replays them with I/O stubbed, then checks output and status consistency. That protects against replay regressions, but it does not define what makes a recommendation good or provide enough coverage to improve the agent deliberately.

A golden dataset should represent the recommendation cases we want the agent to handle well, with enough trace context and expected quality criteria to distinguish valid variation from a regression. It should cover more than exact output matching: recommendation correctness and evidence, a concrete next action, savings consistency, rejected alternatives, provider/resource coverage, and important no-recommendation or edge-case behavior. It must be versioned and maintainable as workflows and models change, without overfitting to one model's wording or one production trace.

Work

  1. Define the golden-dataset contract. Document what qualifies a case for inclusion, what metadata each case carries, and which assertions are exact fields versus rubric/score-based expectations. Include provider, resource/workflow, scenario, expected action/constraints, savings expectations, known edge cases, and the trace/source provenance. Define how to handle valid multiple answers, no-recommendation cases, and cases that become invalid as product behavior changes.

  2. Create the initial dataset. Use the existing golden Langfuse traces as the seed, then expand the set to cover the active recommendation subgraphs and meaningful variation rather than keeping one happy-path trace per workflow. Include successful recommendations, no-recommendation outcomes, hard failures, and successful-but-subtle quality problems that can exercise the evaluator gates. Add enough cases to test the intended rubric across providers/resource types and not just the currently listed AWS examples.

  3. Use it to improve the agent. Run the dataset through the existing black-box replay path (V3WorkflowRunner with deterministic I/O stubs) and the signal-first EvaluationAgent. Record per-case replay status, output comparison, evaluator scores, and the reason a case failed. Turn repeated failures into targeted changes to prompts, candidate generation/validation, selection, or reasoning composition, then rerun the dataset to demonstrate improvement without regressing other cases.

Starting point for quality signals

  • Start with recommendation_actionability_v1 as the broad initial quality signal. It already evaluates generated recommendations with a selected alternative and saved reasoning, and it checks for a concrete, evidence-backed next step.
  • Use recommendation_usability_v4 as a deeper secondary signal and a way to mine difficult cases. It is intentionally gated by static signals such as unusual information retention, high validator waste, or a static "golden" profile, so it should not be the only inclusion criterion or a required score on every case.
  • Treat recommendation_lifecycle_status_v1 as an outcome/stratification label, not a quality definition. It reads the persisted latest recommendation status (DISCOVERED, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED, DISCARDED, or POSTPONED) and can help validate whether recommendations remain useful over time, but lifecycle status alone does not make a trace golden.
  • Pair the LLM signals with deterministic checks already in the evaluator registry, especially static_savings_math_consistency_v1 and static_validator_waste_v2, so a fluent recommendation with inconsistent savings or excessive candidate rejection cannot silently become a golden example.

Acceptance criteria

  • A written rubric defines golden versus excluded cases, required provenance/metadata, coverage dimensions, acceptable output variation, and how the dataset is revised when the agent or product contract changes.
  • A versioned initial dataset exists and is loaded by the eval tests; it is larger and more representative than the current five-trace list, with documented coverage and intentional edge cases.
  • The regression run reports both replay consistency and quality signals per case, including missing/gated scores without treating them as passes.
  • At least one quality assertion uses recommendation_actionability_v1, and the dataset exercises the gated recommendation_usability_v4 path plus deterministic savings/validator checks where applicable.
  • Lifecycle status is available as an outcome label where a persisted recommendation exists, but is not used as the sole golden criterion.
  • The dataset has been used for at least one recommendation-agent improvement iteration, with before/after results showing the targeted quality signal improved without reducing coverage or replay correctness.
items.title: Define and use a golden dataset to improve the recommendation agent

items.content_html:
Context

StaticSavingsMathConsistencyEvaluator already provides the Langfuse trace and score-write infrastructure needed for this work:

  • It is registered in default_recommendation_evaluators().
  • It depends on recommendation_trace_observation and reads the saved recommendation from the terminal handoff_payload.custom_recommendation.
  • It emits ScorePayload objects that EvaluationAgent writes idempotently to the originating Langfuse observation.
  • The existing static_savings_math_consistency_v1 score is the absolute percentage-point gap between the reported and recomputed savings percentage. It is lower-is-better and includes the reported/implied values plus a negative-savings flag in its metadata.

Work

Extend StaticSavingsMathConsistencyEvaluator to emit a second, recommendation-savings score alongside static_savings_math_consistency_v1. Reuse the evaluator's existing calculations and Langfuse write-back path; do not add a separate trace fetcher, evaluator pipeline, or bespoke score-writing path. Keep the existing consistency score and its semantics unchanged.

The new score needs a stable name and explicitly documented range/direction. Its calculation should account for the evaluator's existing resource-specific denominator logic, including the S3 case, and make negative or non-actionable savings visible rather than silently treating them as valid savings.

Acceptance criteria

  • The new score is declared by the evaluator and emitted for the same applicable recommendations as the existing score.
  • The score's formula, range, higher/lower-is-better direction, and handling of negative savings are documented in backend/agents/eval/evaluators/README.md.
  • Score comments/metadata retain enough context to explain the result from the reported percentage, implied percentage, monthly cost, monthly savings, and any negative-savings condition.
  • Unit tests cover consistent and inconsistent percentages, the S3 denominator behavior, negative savings, zero values, and missing recommendation payloads without regressing static_savings_math_consistency_v1.
items.title: Score recommendation savings using evals on Langfuse traces

items.content_html:
Context

The current Cursor error report is centered on workflow_result:failed. That catches hard workflow failures, but it misses the more useful cases: traces tagged workflow_result:generated where a recommendation was produced and the workflow technically succeeded, but the result is still weak or internally inconsistent.

The backend already emits the signals needed to find those cases:

  • recommendation_actionability_v1: a 0-1 judge score for whether the saved reasoning gives a concrete, evidence-backed next step.
  • recommendation_usability_v4: a 0-1 judge score that is intentionally sampled when static signals identify an unusual trace.
  • static_savings_math_consistency_v1: the absolute percentage-point gap between reported and recomputed savings; lower is better, and metadata includes negative-savings state.
  • static_validator_waste_v2: normalized rejected-candidate severity; higher values mean the validator discarded more generated candidates.
  • static_information_retention_v1: a diagnostic signal used with existing thresholds to detect unusually copied or unusually sparse output.
  • static_rejection_reason_concentration_v2: the dominant categorical reason candidates were rejected.

LLMRecommendationUsabilityEvaluator is existing prior art for the combination logic: it gates the judge on high information retention, high validator waste, or a "golden" static profile, rather than treating any single score as a failure. The report should build on those semantics instead of introducing unrelated thresholds.

Work

Include the Langfuse evaluation scores and their comments/metadata in the Cursor error report, but also add trace-level soft-anomaly detection for successful generated recommendations. Scores must be joined by trace/observation so the report can evaluate combinations; workflow-level averages alone are not sufficient.

The report should distinguish:

  1. hard workflow failures (workflow_result:failed), and
  2. successful traces worth reviewing because their score profile is abnormal.

Initial soft-anomaly profiles should include combinations such as:

  • low actionability or usability on a generated recommendation;
  • non-zero savings-math inconsistency, especially with otherwise strong actionability/usability;
  • high validator waste paired with low usability/actionability;
  • unusual information-retention behavior paired with another weak score; and
  • a static "golden" profile that still produces a low usability score.

Reuse the existing score direction and thresholds where they are already defined (ECHO_RETENTION_THRESHOLD, IR_HIGH_THRESHOLD, IR_LOW_THRESHOLD, WASTE_HIGH_THRESHOLD, and the golden-window constants). Calibrate any missing actionability/usability/savings thresholds from generated-trace distributions rather than choosing arbitrary values. A score that was not evaluated because it is sampled or gated must remain explicitly absent/unevaluated, not be treated as a healthy score or an anomaly.

Acceptance criteria

  • The report includes raw score values, score names, comments, and relevant metadata for the associated trace/observation.
  • Successful generated traces are analyzed; the report does not restrict score analysis to failed workflows.
  • Each flagged soft anomaly has a stable reason and includes the score values that triggered it, while hard failures remain separately identifiable.
  • Combination rules are implemented against trace-level data and reuse the evaluator's existing semantics instead of duplicating conflicting thresholds.
  • Tests cover a successful trace with a single weak score, successful traces with the key score combinations above, missing/gated scores, and hard failures.
items.title: Include Langfuse evaluation scores in the Cursor error report

The score should reflect whether recommendations are actionable based on available provider-specific guidance.

items.content_html:
Hi Community! 👋

We want to take a moment to sincerely thank everyone who has participated in the discussions here in the past month. Your comments have been heard and appreciated, and they’ve played a meaningful role in shaping our conversations with our community and products.

To better serve our community and centralize discussions for our product team, we’ve disabled the ability to post on the GitHub Roadmap discussion board. Join us as we continue the conversation in the Community discussions!

The Community discussions are the ideal place to raise feature requests, share feedback, and connect with fellow members. With a dedicated team of community managers and active product managers closely monitoring the forums, this platform ensures better engagement and quicker responses compared to the roadmap discussions.

What’s next?

We have reviewed any user created Discussions and guided to the Community discussions where applicable. We will disable the ability for non GitHub staff to post on GitHub roadmap discussion boards.

Then we will update some roadmap issues with direct links to dedicated feedback discussions where we would love you to upvote and share your feedback where it fits best. Feel free to create a new discussion if needed!

We look forward to hearing your thoughts and engaging with you in the community discussions - see you there!👋

Originally posted by @ankneis in https://github.com/github/roadmap/discussions/1074

items.content_html:
Value Prop

You can now enable and manage auto-merge for stacked pull requests directly in GitHub Mobile on iOS and Android. No more switching to a desktop browser just to configure auto-merge on a stack — everything you need is available right from the stack mergebox in the app. This keeps your workflow moving whether you're at your desk or on the go.

Expected Outcome

Developers working with stacked pull requests gain full auto-merge control on mobile, removing a key gap that previously forced context-switching to desktop. By bringing this capability to the mobile stack mergebox, GitHub Mobile becomes a more complete tool for managing complex review workflows from anywhere.
items.title: GitHub Mobile: Auto-merge support for Stacked PRs [GA]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

You can now rebase an entire stack of pull requests directly from GitHub Mobile, without needing to switch to a desktop browser. Track rebase progress and status in real time from the stack merge section, so you stay in control of your stacked pull request workflows wherever you are.

Expected Outcome

Developers working with stacked pull requests often hit blockers when branches fall out of date—and resolving them previously required leaving the mobile experience entirely. This release brings full rebase support to GitHub Mobile, helping teams keep their stacks current and their momentum going, even when they're away from their desks.
items.title: GitHub Mobile: Rebase Stacked PRs [GA]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

You can now attach local images and videos directly to issues, pull requests, and comments using the GitHub CLI. This works across gh issue create, gh issue comment, gh pr create, gh pr comment, and gh pr edit.

Expected Outcome

Developers and teams using GitHub CLI in automated or agentic workflows gain a reliable way to include visual evidence like screenshots, recordings, and diagrams alongside their work. This closes a long-standing gap that made it difficult to provide proof of work or communicate changes clearly through the CLI alone. The result is a more complete CLI experience that fits naturally into both human and agentic development flows.
items.title: GitHub CLI: Image upload and attach for issues, PRs, and comments [GA]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

Enterprise administrators and billing managers can now set hard spending limits on Copilot licenses at the enterprise and organization level, giving them the same budget enforcement capabilities already available for usage-based products like Actions and Codespaces. Instead of relying on soft limits and email notifications that only alert when thresholds are reached, admins can enforce strict caps that prevent teams from exceeding their allocated Copilot budget. This eliminates surprise overages, simplifies financial governance across large organizations, and gives IT leaders confidence that individual business units will only consume the licenses they've been allocated.

Expected Outcome

Large enterprises managing Copilot across multiple organizations need predictable, enforceable spending controls. Today, license-based products only support soft limits — admins receive notifications at 75%, 90%, and 100% thresholds but the platform does not prevent overages. This gap forces billing managers to manually monitor and intervene, creating operational overhead and financial risk. By introducing hard budgets for Copilot License SKUs, we enable enterprises to set organization-level license caps that are automatically enforced, ensuring each business unit stays within its purchased allocation. This reduces administrative burden, prevents unintentional overuse by one organization at the expense of others, and removes a key blocker for enterprises scaling Copilot adoption with confidence.
items.title: Copilot SKU-level hard budgets [GA]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

Proof of Presence requires developers to re-authenticate through their organization's identity provider before completing high-impact actions like merging or approving pull requests. This protection now works across all major SSO providers—including Okta, Ping, and any SAML or OIDC-compatible IdP—so every team benefits regardless of which identity provider they use. Organizations get stronger, identity-backed verification at the moments that matter most, powered by their existing MFA setup.

Expected Outcome

With Proof of Presence generally available across all identity providers, organizations can consistently enforce re-authentication at critical points in the software development lifecycle. Routing verification through each team's own IdP and MFA gives security teams confidence that only authorized contributors can merge or approve code changes. This reduces the risk of unauthorized changes from compromised accounts and helps teams meet security and compliance requirements without adding unnecessary friction to everyday workflows.
items.title: Proof of Presence (PoP) – General Availability across all identity providers [GA]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

When a repository policy requires it, developers approving or merging a pull request are prompted to complete a fresh, interactive MFA challenge through Microsoft Entra ID before the action goes through. This ensures that the specific person taking those high-impact actions is genuinely present and verified at the exact moment they matter — not just holding an active session. It adds a meaningful layer of identity assurance directly into the pull request workflow, without changing how teams collaborate day to day.

Expected Outcome

Regulated organizations can now demonstrate, with a real-time identity check, that pull request approvals and merges were performed by an authorized, present individual — strengthening compliance with requirements like FDA 21 CFR Part 11. By anchoring proof of presence to the two most consequential points in the code review process, teams reduce the risk that compromised tokens or sessions could silently influence what ships to production.
items.title: Proof of Presence (PoP) for Pull Requests – Re-authentication on PR merge & approval (Entra IdP) [Public Preview]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

Enterprises using Microsoft Entra ID can now require users to complete a fresh, interactive MFA challenge through their own identity provider before performing sensitive actions on GitHub. Re-authentication is driven by your existing Entra ID configuration—whether SAML or OIDC—so there's no new tooling to set up and no changes to how your teams authenticate day-to-day. This gives security and compliance teams stronger assurance that a real, authorized person is behind every high-impact operation.

Expected Outcome

Long-lived session tokens are a known vector for supply-chain attacks, and organizations subject to strict compliance requirements need more than a valid session cookie to authorize consequential actions. By tying re-authentication directly to the moment of action—and routing the challenge through the customer's own IdP—GitHub helps enterprises reduce exposure from compromised credentials while satisfying regulatory and internal security mandates. The result is a tighter, verifiable link between identity and action across your GitHub environment.
items.title: Proof of Presence (PoP) – Interactive re-authentication for high-impact actions (Entra IdP) [Public Preview]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

Enterprise owners and security admins can now export a complete inventory of every credential in their enterprise — including SSH keys, personal access tokens, OAuth app tokens, and GitHub App tokens — from a single view in the UI or via REST API. Each credential entry includes rich metadata like the owner, scopes, creation and expiration dates, last-used timestamp, source IP, and target organizations and repositories. This gives security teams everything they need to assess risk, respond to incidents, and meet compliance requirements on their own terms.

Expected Outcome

Organizations gain direct, self-serve visibility into all credentials active within their enterprise, eliminating the blind spots that slow down incident response and force reliance on GitHub Support for data they should own. Admins can quickly identify exposed tokens, scope the impact of a security event, and take remediation actions — such as bulk revocations or SSO deauthorizations — without external assistance. This positions GitHub as a meaningful choice for regulated industries and security-conscious enterprises that require strong credential governance.
items.title: Enterprise-level credential visibility - List/Export inventory of all token types [GA]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22 brings the latest GitHub capabilities to your self-hosted environment, giving your teams access to new features and improvements without moving your data to the cloud. Whether you need tighter control over your infrastructure, compliance with data residency requirements, or simply want to run GitHub on your own terms, this release keeps you current with the tools developers rely on every day.

Expected Outcome

This release delivers a supported, production-ready version of GitHub Enterprise Server that organizations can deploy with confidence. Teams running self-hosted GitHub infrastructure can adopt the newest platform improvements while maintaining the security, compliance, and operational standards their environments require.
items.title: GHES 3.22 [GA]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

Secrets don’t respect boundaries; scanning for them shouldn’t either.

GitHub monitors the entire public surface of github.com for leaked secrets in real time. Public monitoring attributes those secrets back to your enterprise, based on where your people commit.

Expected Outcome

Secret scanning has always protected the repositories you own. But secrets leak beyond that boundary. For example, a developer commits to a personal fork or an open source project, or they paste a token into a public issue or pull request, and this often happens from an account your security team isn’t tracking. Exposures like these were nearly impossible to find and often only surfaced after they’d been abused by bad actors.

Public monitoring closes that gap. It finds these vulnerabilities and attributes them to your enterprise so you can respond quickly. The feature scans for secrets exposed anywhere in public content across github.com—including git content, pull request comments, and GitHub issues—and natively attributes each one back to your enterprise, through GitHub’s identity layer and verified domains.

Because the activity happens on GitHub, so does the attribution: in real time (not a nightly async crawl), definitively with native platform metadata (not on a guess from a commit email), and across arbitrary public repositories (not just surfaces where you tell us to look).

Public monitoring will never scan private repositories; it surfaces only secrets that are already exposed publicly, so you can revoke leaked secrets before they’re abused by bad actors. The feature is available at no additional cost for enterprises with GitHub Secret Protection.
items.title: Public Monitoring For Enterprises [General Availability]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

Upgrading GitHub Enterprise Server now requires about 20 minutes less downtime. Starting with GHES 3.21, pre-upgrade steps that previously ran during the maintenance window can now be run beforehand, while the appliance is still serving traffic.

Expected Outcome

Downtime during upgrades is one of the most significant friction points for GHES customers. Starting in 3.21, the pre-upgrade steps run while the appliance is still live, moving ~20 minutes of work outside the maintenance window and reducing total downtime accordingly.
items.title: Reduce Downtime through Upgrade Orchestration [GA]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

These GitHub Actions updates give you sharper visibility and tighter control over your CI/CD workflows. A new REST API lets your team check runner version deprecation timelines before they become a problem, while a new vulnerability-alerts read permission for GITHUB_TOKEN enables least-privilege access to Dependabot alerts. Four new job context properties also make it easier for reusable workflows to know their own source identity at runtime — so your shared workflows can reference exactly where they came from.

Expected Outcome

Teams that rely on GitHub Actions can proactively plan runner upgrades instead of reacting to deprecation notices, reducing disruption to their pipelines. Finer-grained token permissions help organizations enforce security best practices without sacrificing access to the data their workflows need. Reusable workflow authors gain the runtime context they need to build more self-aware, maintainable automation.
items.title: GitHub Actions: Early August 2026 Updates [GA]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

Actions Runner Controller (ARC) 0.15.0 makes it easier to configure, operate, and troubleshoot self-hosted runners on Kubernetes — with cleaner Helm chart configuration, improved logging, and a batch of fixes and improvements requested directly by the ARC community. Platform teams spend less time wrestling with rough edges and more time shipping. This release incorporates vetted community contributions, so the improvements reflect real-world usage at scale.

Expected Outcome

Teams running GitHub Actions on Kubernetes gain a more stable and polished ARC experience, with fewer day-to-day friction points and better visibility when things go wrong. By consistently addressing community-reported issues and merging community pull requests, this release builds confidence in the ARC release cadence and migration path away from legacy ARC.
items.title: Actions Runner Controller 0.15.0 [GA]

items.content_html:
Value Prop

GitHub Enterprise Server is removing an unused service, Node Eligibility Service (NES), to keep the platform lean and well-maintained. This cleanup reduces unnecessary complexity in your self-hosted environment without affecting any customer-facing functionality.

Expected Outcome

Retiring this service eliminates dead code and maintenance burden that provided no customer value.
items.title: Retire Node Eligibility Service (NES) [Closing Down]
